prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: After the full first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B059, Katori and Ye. Four members prefer it, three more list it as an alternative, and the chair's synthesis shows that nobody questions the physics. That is not why I keep it; the reasons are scientific. The magic-wavelength idea is a single, simple and slightly surprising observation: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift of the two clock levels is equal, and the lattice stops disturbing the very transition it holds. That removes Doppler and recoil effects and lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once. It was then realised, and the realisation was pushed to the 10^-18 frontier, and several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reproduce and compare the clocks, with millimetre-scale gravitational redshifts as a visible consequence. Theory and measurement agree closely on the systematic shifts, which is the quality I weigh most. In answer to the chair's first question, I think the citation can state the distinction from 2005 and 2012 plainly: the comb prize rewarded the readout of an optical oscillation, the 2012 prize rewarded control of one trapped quantum system, and the lattice clock is a different solution to a different problem, namely many atoms with all the leading shifts cancelled together. My proposed wording rests on the lattice clock itself and does not mention the comb. On the second question, I have no reason from what I have read to add names beyond Katori and Ye, but I accept that the committee should verify the 2003 to 2006 record. On the third, the redefinition of the second is a signal of maturity, not a reason to wait: the clocks have already met the criterion that independent devices agree at 10^-18, and the redefinition is a later administrative step by the metrology community that we do not need to anticipate.
statement.case_against: The objection that I take most seriously is still the overlap. A sceptic can read the lattice clock as the best application of tools honoured in 2005 and 2012, and Olsson's point that a prize should not go to the second person who did it better applies to part of Ye's contribution. If a majority concludes that this is a refinement and not a new achievement, my case fails. The second reservation is credit: Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow and Takamoto may have claims that I cannot weigh from my own knowledge of the primary record, and it is possible that the record of 2003 to 2006 shows a more shared origin than I believe. Finally, much of the societal payoff (redefined second, geodesy, dark-matter searches) is still in the future. I have also noted that I am an atomic theorist, so I may be inclined to like the elegance of a precision experiment more than a particle physicist or condensed-matter colleague would.

responses.point: Olsson accepts B059 but says the Katori and Ye boundary needs a check against the 2003 to 2006 record, that Katori proposed and first demonstrated the strontium lattice clock while Ye's decisive step is performance and many-body clock physics, and that the citation should say invention and development.
responses.response: I accept your wording and have used it: the citation now says invention and development. I agree the boundary is where the credit test bites, and I would state it in the committee's own terms. Katori holds the concept and the first realisation, and Ye holds the demonstration that the concept reaches 10^-18 and the use of the clock as a controlled many-body system. I do not read that as a second discoverer doing it better, because the step to 10^-18 required new control of density shifts, coherence and blackbody effects, and the physics that came out of it (spin-orbit and many-body interactions inside the lattice clock) was not in the original proposal. I still think an outside check of the 2003 to 2006 priority record is cheap and sensible, and I would support asking for it, but I do not expect it to produce a third name.

responses.point: Johansson moved his first choice from circuit QED to B059, gave the distinctness test as tools and a different architecture versus a clock that solves Doppler, recoil and Stark shifts together, and asked me whether Ye's credit belongs to the lattice clock or partly to the comb-linked work already honoured.
responses.response: You asked for a direct answer, so here it is. Ye's comb and cavity-stabilisation work was honoured by the 2005 prize through Hall, and I would not credit it again. The credit I propose for Ye is limited to the strontium lattice clock: the accuracy and stability work that took it to 10^-18, and the clock as a many-body system. That is separable from the comb in the same way a spectrometer's performance is separable from the laser that drives it, and the citation says nothing about the comb. If a colleague can show that the decisive step to 10^-18 was in fact a comb or laser-stabilisation advance and not a lattice-clock advance, I would reconsider the pairing and tell you. I agree with your reading of why I hold B013 as a first alternative; I fully understand your recusal position there and I would not ask you to argue it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B034 but says his fifth rank for B059 reflects deference to atomic physicists and that he would rank it higher if Kroll and I think it is clearly distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; he accepts naming Jarillo-Herrero over his students.
responses.response: You asked me directly about distinctness, and I think it is clearly distinct on the physics: neither the frequency comb nor single-ion control gives a way to hold thousands of neutral atoms with all leading shifts cancelled, and the answer to that problem is the magic wavelength. I also take your offer seriously on B034. I agree the prediction followed by observation is the pattern I admire, and the argument about Jarillo-Herrero is a fair one for the statutes. My remaining worry is the one you list yourself: the pairing mechanism is open, and several colleagues, including Mehlig and Kroll, describe sample dependence as still real after eight years. I would prefer to see that settle, and a prize now would fix the narrative before the physics has. I keep B034 as a candidate that could be a strong one in a later year, and I respect that you hold it first.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B016 because the Z2 mechanism is identified and understood, and argues that the 2016 topological-phases prize covers the integer quantum Hall lineage and not the time-reversal-invariant case; he also says the overlap with 2005 and 2012 makes the clock step smaller than it looks.
responses.response: On B016 I agree with the substance of your argument: the 2016 citation does not decide for me that the Z2 insulator is already honoured, and I said so in my reading. The mechanism is understood, and the experiment on HgTe could have failed. My difficulty is that the credit problem seems sharper than you allow: Mele is an author of the founding paper, but Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp tested, and Hasan's three-dimensional work is outside the cap. A three-name prize on that boundary will be read as a ruling between living claimants, whereas the clock case has two names that every member who proposed laureates gave. On the clock overlap, the same maturity test you apply to B016 (mechanism understood, independent confirmation) is met in B059 and the step is a different one from the comb. I regard B016 as the strongest condensed-matter case here and would not oppose it as an alternative.

responses.point: Kroll shares the clock case but asks that the Katori and Ye boundary and the Lemonde, Gill and Bloom claims be checked against the primary record, and discloses a year in Hall's laboratory, in the lineage in which Ye worked.
responses.response: I agree that the primary-record check is the committee's responsibility, and I withdraw the impression I gave in round 1 that it is not needed: I said I do not expect a third name, but I should have said I would not decide it from memory. On the Hall lineage, I do not think it requires recusal: your link is to the comb-era laboratory and not to the lattice clock, and the citation I propose avoids the comb. It is your decision to make and the chair's to rule on, and I think it is enough that it is disclosed. On the redefinition of the second, I disagree with Mehlig's reading that it adds nothing scientifically, but I agree with you that it should not decide the outcome either way.

uncertainties: Whether the primary record of 2003 to 2006 supports Katori and Ye alone or gives Lemonde, Gill, Bloom or others a claim that a two-name prize would unfairly ignore; I do not know the history of lattice clocks as precisely as I know atomic structure theory, and I would want an outside check.
Whether a majority will regard the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes or as a refinement of them; my reading of that question is a judgement, not a measurement.
Whether Ye's credit is best stated for the lattice clock alone, and whether Katori's first demonstrations were truly ahead of the other groups.
My assessment of twisted bilayer graphene, topological insulators, the Higgs boson and IceCube rests on deference to colleagues whose fields I know less well.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I have no known personal, institutional or collaborative connection with Katori or Ye or with any other credited name on the shortlist. I have worked closely with the Lund attosecond group (L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate) and with Keller's group at ETH, but neither is a candidate on this shortlist. I am a theoretical atomic physicist in the same broad community as the clock groups, and I have no recusal on B059 to report, though I note that general closeness for transparency. After reading Kroll's disclosure I note that I have no link to the Hall laboratory. I have no ties to B013, B022 or any other part that I mention as an alternative, beyond field proximity for B022.
